666.title: Sita goes home to the earth
666.hook: Sita's last oath, and why Hindus say her name before Rama's
666.carry: sita is a goddess, named before rama
666.tomorrow: the poets loved this story. did they keep her ending?
666.howItsDone: Sita's return to the earth is told in Hindu homes, songs and stage plays, often with deep grief for her; devotees honor Sita as a goddess in her own right, linked with the earth and with Lakshmi, and many greet each other with 'Sita Ram' or 'Jai Siya Ram', her name first.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kusha and Lava, named for a handful of grass, singing their father's story before him without knowing it. Today, the last time Sita stands before Rama.
screen: `TWO BOYS SING TO THEIR FATHER.`

segments.voice: Sita's name means furrow. Back in the first book, King Janaka was plowing a field for a ritual when the plow turned up a baby girl in the earth. He raised her as his daughter and named her for the furrow. Hold on to that, because the Ramayana remembers it. Today the girl from the furrow, now the mother of two grown boys, is brought before a great assembly and asked, one more time, to prove herself.
screen: `SITA MEANS FURROW.` → `FOUND IN A PLOWED FIELD.` → `ASKED ONCE MORE TO PROVE HERSELF.`

segments.voice: When Rama learns the singing boys are his sons, he sends word to Valmiki: if Sita is pure, let her come and swear it here, before everyone. The next morning the assembly fills: sages, kings, ordinary people. Valmiki walks in first, and Sita follows, head bowed. These are your sons, Valmiki tells Rama, and Sita is blameless; he stakes on it all the merit of his long life. Rama answers that he believes it, and that he sent her away because of what people were saying. But the oath is still asked of her. Then Sita speaks. If I have never thought of anyone but Rama, let the earth goddess open and give me a place. If I have honored him in mind, word and deed, let the earth receive me. The ground splits. A shining throne rises, held up by serpents, and the earth goddess takes Sita in her arms and seats her there. The throne sinks, and the earth closes. Rama is wild with grief. The girl from the furrow has gone home to her mother. Now, here's what Hindus did with that ending. They didn't remember Sita as a woman who lost. They worship her. Many honor her as Lakshmi, the goddess, come down beside Vishnu's avatar, and in the Ram darbar picture in many homes she sits at Rama's side. Listen to how people greet each other in much of North India: Sita Ram, or Jai Siya Ram. Her name comes first, the way devotees also say Radha Krishna and Gauri Shankar. Many explain it simply: the Goddess, the mother, is named first.

segments.voice: If you can, put your bare feet flat on the ground, or sit on the floor, and feel your weight handed down into the earth. The ground is holding you. If you pray, say Sita Ram softly on each out-breath, to the earth's daughter. If you don't, just thank the ground for holding you up.

667.title: Many Ramayanas
667.hook: poets who loved Sita's story told her ending three different ways
667.carry: hari katha ananta: god's stories never end
667.tomorrow: was Rama right to send Sita away?
667.howItsDone: Hindu communities meet the Ramayana through many retellings at once, Valmiki's Sanskrit, Kamban's Tamil, Tulsidas's Hindi and others, and families discuss Sita's exile openly, with different views at the same table.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the girl from the furrow went home, and your line was Sita is a goddess, named before Rama. Today, what the poets did with her ending.
screen: `SITA IS A GODDESS, NAMED BEFORE RAMA.`

segments.voice: A poet sits with a pen in the air. The poet loves this story, knows it by heart, and is retelling it for a new audience, in a new language, long after Valmiki. Now the ending has come: Sita's exile, and the earth opening. Tell it as it came down? Change it? Or quietly put the pen down before getting there? Real poets faced exactly this choice, and they didn't all choose the same way.
screen: `A POET, LONG AFTER VALMIKI.` → `YOU REACH THE ENDING.` → `TELL IT, CHANGE IT, OR STOP?`

segments.voice: Start with Bhavabhuti, a Sanskrit playwright. His play is called the Uttararamacharita, the later story of Rama. He follows the exile closely and lets Rama's grief run deep. But in the final act, Valmiki stages a play for Rama, a play about Sita, and when it ends, the earth goddess and the river Ganga bring Sita back, and husband and wife are reunited. Bhavabhuti changed the ending, on purpose. Then there's Kamban, who sang the Ramayana in Tamil. His great poem closes with Rama's crowning; it doesn't go on into the later book. And Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, a form of Hindi, still recited across North India. His last section is also called the Uttar Kand, but it isn't a story of Sita's exile; it's mostly teaching and devotion. Keep the hard ending, rewrite it toward reunion, or end at the crowning. None of these poets stands outside the faith looking in; the tradition treasures all three. And Tulsidas gives the reason in his own poem: Hari is endless, and Hari's stories are endless, hari ananta, hari katha ananta, and the saints tell them and hear them in many ways. Hindus don't keep one sealed Ramayana. They keep a living one, retold in Sanskrit and Tamil and Hindi and Bengali, on village stages and on television, and the retelling itself is devotion. That's why a grandmother's Ramayana and a new picture book can differ, and both still be prayer.

668.title: Was Rama right?
668.hook: a king's duty against Sita's innocence, and why dharma is called subtle
668.carry: dharma is subtle: even good duties collide
668.tomorrow: how does the Ramayana end, and who stays behind?
668.howItsDone: Hindu teachers, storytellers and families discuss Sita's exile openly: some defend Rama's choice as a king's duty, some grieve it as a wrong done to Sita, and women's folk songs in several languages sing her side.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SIXTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uttararamacharita and the poets' choices, and your line: hari katha ananta, God's stories never end. Today, the two sides of the argument itself.
screen: `HARI KATHA ANANTA.`

segments.voice: A Ramayana play has ended, and a family is still at the dinner table. An uncle says Rama did the right thing: a king belongs to his people first. An aunt puts down her spoon and says Sita did nothing wrong, and she was sent away pregnant into a forest. A teenager asks why nobody asked Sita. Each of them is drawing on the tradition. Today, the strongest form of each side, Sita's own words, and why Hindus have never settled it.
screen: `AFTER THE PLAY, AT THE TABLE.` → `HE WAS A KING FIRST.` → `SHE DID NOTHING WRONG.`

segments.voice: The first side rests on rajadharma, the duty of a king. In this reading, Rama's private life is not his own. A king who keeps what he loves while his people lose faith in him has failed the kingdom, so Rama gives up what is dearest to him, and the poem shows him suffering for it. Readers on this side honor the exile as a terrible sacrifice made by both of them. The second side starts from Sita. She was already tested by fire, in the war book, and found pure. She is pregnant. She is sent away without a hearing, by a husband who knows she's innocent. Readers on this side, devotees of Rama among them, call it a wound in the story. And then there are Sita's own words. When Lakshmana leaves her at the Ganga, Valmiki gives her a message to send back. She knows she is blameless. She carries his child. And she asks Rama to care for the people of the city as he would his own brothers. No shouting; a great deal of dignity. Why can't the tradition settle it? Because Hinduism has a word for this kind of knot. Dharma, right action, is called subtle. In the Mahabharata, when Draupadi asks a hall of elders whether she was lost fairly, the great Bhishma answers that the way of dharma is subtle, and he cannot untie it. Rama's duty as a king and his duty as a husband are both dharma, and here they pull apart. The faith doesn't hide the knot. It keeps both readings inside, and asks you to think.
screen: `RAJADHARMA: THE KING'S DUTY.` · `SITA: BLAMELESS, PREGNANT, UNHEARD.` · `HER OWN MESSAGE BACK TO RAMA.` · `BHISHMA: DHARMA IS SUBTLE.` · then, large: `EVEN GOOD DUTIES COLLIDE.`

segments.voice: Think of a real disagreement with someone you care about. For one breath, argue their side as well as you can; for the next, your own. Go back and forth a few times without picking a winner. If you pray, ask for viveka, clear discernment; if you don't, simply let both sides rest and breathe.

669.tomorrow: why do Hindus wait up till midnight for a baby?
669.howItsDone: Many Hindu households recite the Ramayana or its Sundara Kanda on special occasions, and at many readings a seat is kept for Hanuman, who is said to listen wherever Rama's story is told; the later book is read, told or argued over in many different ways.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SIXTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, rajadharma, and your line: dharma is subtle, even good duties collide. Today, the last day of the Ramayana serial.
screen: `DHARMA IS SUBTLE.`

segments.voice: Months ago, at the start of this serial, by a river, a hunter's arrow brought down a bird, and Valmiki's grief turned into the first verse. Since then: a bow broken at a wedding, a forest, a golden deer, a leap across the sea, a war, a homecoming, and a later book that won't let the homecoming be the end. Today, how the poem itself finally stops, and who it leaves behind.
screen: `MONTHS AGO, A BIRD'S CRY.` → `A WEDDING, A WAR, A HOMECOMING.` → `WHO STAYS BEHIND?`

segments.voice: After Sita is gone, Valmiki's poem goes on a little longer. Rama rules alone, for many years. Back when he was crowned, he had said goodbye to his allies one by one, and when it was Hanuman's turn, Hanuman asked for only one thing. Let my love for you never waver, he said, and let me live on earth as long as your story is told. Rama granted it. Now Rama's own time on earth is complete. He walks out of Ayodhya toward the river Sarayu, and the people of the city follow him, unwilling to stay behind. He walks into the water, and returns to his own form as Vishnu. That's the last image: a king walking into a river. But one devotee doesn't follow. Rama reminds Hanuman of his wish: stay, as long as my story is told. So the Ramayana ends with a gift. Wherever it's recited, devotees believe Hanuman is listening. That's why, at many Ramayana readings, people keep a seat empty for him, sometimes with a cloth and a flower on it. And it's the deeper reason the story is still told, even with an ending people argue over. For devotees, telling it isn't only remembering. It's a place where God's greatest devotee is present, and through him, Rama. The avatar went home. The story stayed, and Hanuman stayed with it. Many teachers read Hanuman as bhakti, loving devotion, at its plainest: a love that asks only to stay near God's name. So when a grandmother reads the Ramayana aloud in a living room, devotees would say that room isn't ordinary anymore.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sarayu, and your line: where Rama's story is told, Hanuman is there. Today, a new block begins: the festival year.
screen: `WHERE RAMA'S STORY IS TOLD, HANUMAN IS THERE.`

segments.voice: It's nearly midnight, and in temples across India, and in living rooms in Houston and Leicester and Singapore, people who have fasted all day are waiting. There's a small cradle decorated with flowers. At twelve, the conch shells blow, the bells ring, and somebody sets a tiny image of a baby into the cradle and starts rocking it. A birthday, kept at the exact hour. Why midnight? The answer starts in a prison cell.
screen: `A DAY OF FASTING.` → `AN EMPTY CRADLE.` → `AT MIDNIGHT, THE CONCH.`

segments.voice: Janma means birth. Ashtami means the eighth: the eighth day of the waning moon. The story is told in the tenth book of the Bhagavata Purana. In Mathura, the tyrant Kamsa is driving his cousin Devaki and her new husband Vasudeva after their wedding, when a voice from the sky tells him: the eighth child of this woman will kill you. Kamsa locks them in prison. Child after child is born there, and Kamsa kills them; the seventh, the text says, is carried away to another womb. Then comes the eighth. He is born at midnight, and the Bhagavata says the whole world grows calm and bright at that hour. The baby first appears to his parents in a divine form, then becomes an ordinary newborn. Vasudeva's chains fall away. The guards sleep. The doors open by themselves. Vasudeva lifts the baby and walks out into a storm. The great serpent Shesha spreads its hoods over them. At the Yamuna, swollen with rain, the river gives way. In Gokul, the cowherd Nanda's wife Yashoda has just given birth. Vasudeva leaves his son there and carries her baby back. This is the heart of a big Hindu teaching: avatara, God coming down. In the Bhagavad Gita, the grown Krishna says it himself: whenever dharma declines and wrong rises, I come, age after age, to protect the good. So people don't stay up only for a birthday. They stay up for that promise, kept in the darkest hour, in the most locked-up place.
screen: `JANMA: BIRTH. ASHTAMI: THE EIGHTH.` · `THE EIGHTH CHILD, BORN IN A PRISON.` · `THE CHAINS FALL. THE RIVER GIVES WAY.` · `AVATARA: GOD COMES DOWN.` · then, large: `IN THE DARKEST HOUR.`

segments.voice: Dim the lights or close your eyes, and sit in the dark without hurrying it. If you pray, softly say Krishna's name, or the line many sing at midnight: Nand ke anand bhayo, jai Kanhaiya Lal ki, joy in Nanda's house. If you don't, simply wait for something good, the way people wait for twelve.
Janmashtami. The birthday on the eighth: Krishna born at midnight in Kamsa's prison, God come down, kept by many Hindus with a fast and a cradle.
screen: `JANMASHTAMI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: avatara, God comes down in the darkest hour. Tomorrow, a guest made of clay. That's day six hundred seventy.

671.title: Ganesh Chaturthi: the guest who wants love
671.hook: Ganesha comes home as a guest, and a handful of rice beats a feast
671.carry: god accepts what's offered with love
671.tomorrow: who is the Goddess the gods couldn't win without?
671.howItsDone: Families bring a clay Ganesha home on Ganesh Chaturthi, install and worship it for one and a half to ten days with flowers, durva grass, modaks and aarti, then carry it in procession to water for immersion; many cities also hold large public pandals.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janmashtami, a baby born at midnight in a prison. Your line was avatara, God comes down in the darkest hour. Today, a guest arrives.
screen: `AVATARA: GOD COMES DOWN.`

segments.voice: In cities across Maharashtra, in late summer, you'll see something like a parade and a house move at once. A family walks down the street with drums and cymbals, and in the middle, carried in someone's arms or in a car with the windows down, is a clay Ganesha, garlanded, sometimes taller than the person carrying him. He's coming to stay: for a day and a half, or five days, or ten. And when he leaves, he'll be carried to the water.
screen: `DRUMS IN THE STREET.` → `A CLAY GANESHA, CARRIED HOME.` → `AND THEN, TO THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Chaturthi means the fourth: the fourth day of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada, usually in August or September. It's kept as Ganesha's birthday. For these days he is treated exactly like an honored guest. In a rite called pranapratishtha, establishing the breath of life, the family invites him into the clay image. Then he's welcomed the way you'd welcome family off a long trip: a seat, water, flowers, red hibiscus and durva grass, modaks, songs morning and evening. That's not only a festival custom. It's how Hindu worship, puja, is built: God received as a guest. And a story families love to tell, told many ways and not from the oldest texts, says what this guest really wants. Kubera, the god of wealth, throws a grand feast to show off his riches, and Ganesha comes as the guest. Ganesha eats. And eats. The kitchens empty, and he's still hungry, until Kubera runs, embarrassed, to Shiva. Kubera is given one handful of roasted rice and told to offer it humbly. He does, and Ganesha is full at last. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna teaches the same thing in plain words: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, offered with love, I accept. So a family with a small clay Ganesha and one plate of modaks hasn't done less than the giant public pandals that grew from Pune in the 1890s. On the last day the guest is thanked and carried to the water: visarjan, letting go. The love was the offering all along.
screen: `CHATURTHI: THE FOURTH DAY.` · `PUJA: GOD RECEIVED AS A GUEST.` · `KUBERA'S FEAST CAN'T FILL HIM.` · `A HANDFUL OF RICE, GIVEN HUMBLY.` · then, large: `OFFERED WITH LOVE, ACCEPTED.`

segments.voice: Take one small thing, a flower, a sweet, a glass of water, and set it in front of a picture of Ganesha, or anywhere quiet. Offer it slowly, as to a guest you love. If you pray, say Om Gam Ganapataye Namah once. If you don't, offer it in thanks to someone who has fed you.
Ganesh Chaturthi. Ganesha's fourth day: a clay guest welcomed home, offered what the family has with love, and given back to the water.

segments.voice: Your line: God accepts what's offered with love. A handful of rice was enough. Until tomorrow.

672.title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
672.hook: the gods' light becomes the Goddess; nine nights honoring Shakti, God as Mother
672.carry: shakti: the divine mother is the power in all
672.howItsDone: During autumn Navaratri, many Hindus honor the Goddess for nine nights with fasting, recitation of the Devi Mahatmya, garba and dandiya dancing around her lamp in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal, and golu doll displays in the South, ending with Vijayadashami on the tenth day.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesh Chaturthi, a clay guest welcomed home. Your line was God accepts what's offered with love. Today, a war the gods have already lost.
screen: `GOD ACCEPTS WHAT'S OFFERED WITH LOVE.`

segments.voice: The gods have lost. Not a skirmish: the whole war. A demon king named Mahisha, who can take the shape of a buffalo, has beaten them, thrown them out of heaven and taken their seats. They go, humiliated, to Vishnu and Shiva and tell them everything. And as they tell it, something happens that nobody plans. Their anger starts to glow. That's how the Devi Mahatmya, the great text of the Goddess, opens the battle it's known for.
screen: `THE GODS HAVE LOST.` → `MAHISHA TAKES HEAVEN.` → `THEIR ANGER STARTS TO GLOW.`

segments.voice: From the faces of Vishnu, Shiva and Brahma, and then from all the gods, a great light pours out, tejas, the text calls it, radiance, and it gathers into one blaze like a mountain on fire. The blaze takes the form of a woman: the Goddess. Every god gives her something: Shiva a trident, Vishnu a discus, the mountain Himalaya a lion to ride. She laughs, and the sound shakes the worlds. Then she goes to war with Mahisha. He fights her as a buffalo, then a lion, then a man with a sword, then an elephant, then a buffalo again. She pins him under her foot and ends him. Behind this story is one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: Shakti. The Goddess isn't a helper the gods made. She is their power, gathered into one, and many Hindus worship God as Mother. A hymn later in the same text, sung in many homes at Navaratri, praises her as the Goddess who dwells in all beings as power, as mind, as compassion, as mother. Some teachers read Mahisha, the shape-shifter, as the ego that keeps changing form; that's a reading, not the text. Navaratri means nine nights: nava, nine, ratri, night. For nine nights in autumn, many Hindus honor the Goddess. In Gujarat, people dance garba in circles around her lamp until late. In Bengal, it's Durga Puja. In much of the South, families set up golu, steps of dolls. On the tenth day, Vijayadashami, the day of victory, the good has won.
screen: `THE GODS' RADIANCE BECOMES ONE.` · `THE GODDESS, ARMED BY ALL.` · `SHAKTI: GOD AS MOTHER.` · `NAVA RATRI: NINE NIGHTS.` · then, large: `THE POWER IN ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: Sit tall, and say slowly, or just listen inside to, the line many sing at Navaratri: ya devi sarvabhuteshu shakti rupena samsthita. To the Goddess who dwells in all beings as power. Feel your own strength as something given. If you don't pray, simply name one strength you've been given, and say thank you.
Navaratri. Nine nights honoring the Goddess, Shakti, who defeated Mahisha, ending on the tenth day, the day of victory.
